newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Hashimoto seeks to craft reformist image.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto seeks to craft reformist image.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has been quick off the mark at the start of his second term to promote an image as a bold reformer, but sceptics are still wondering -- can a leopard change its spots?

Just days after being sworn in as head of his new all Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) cabinet, Hashimoto on Monday unveiled sweeping proposals to liberalise Japan's lagging financial markets by the year 2001.
On Tuesday he ordered his trade minister to draft radical reforms to ensure the economy flourishes in the 21st century.
But the start of Hashimoto's new administration has also been marred by a whiff of scandal, a reminder of the old-style money politics that is the legacy of decades of LDP rule.

Hashimoto's LDP expanded its seats in parliament's Lower House in an election last month but fell 12 short of a majority, forcing it to form a minority government backed by a loose alliance with two former coalition partners.
The conservative party's return to sole power after being booted out in 1993 left many worried about prospects for change given its close ties with vested interests and bureaucrats.
Scepticism still abounds, despite Hashimoto's announcement of what officials dubbed a "Big Bang" financial reform package.
Many of the ideas have been floated for years and are under discussion by advisory panels. Opposition from specific financial sectors expected to suffer is likely to be fierce.
Ironically, however, it may turn out to be the conservative old-guard that succeeds where self-styled reformers failed.
"The paradox is you've got an old guard that now has a consensus and the ability to get things done," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.

"Yes, the legacy of old-style money politics is strong within the LDP...but rather than just getting entrapped in the past, Hashimoto is trying to move ahead," Koll said. "Japan is very good at a revolution from within, that's what it has been doing since the Meiji Restoration."
Japan's 1868 Meiji Restoration ushered in broad political, social and economic changes which resulted in a modern, unified Japanese state, open to Western influence and trade.
So far, a tax evasion scandal with political overtones does not look set to do serious damage to Hashimoto's cabinet.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka on Tuesday acknowledged that the LDP faction he heads received political donations from an oil trader at the centre of the affair, but said the donations were legal and proper and did not constitute a bribe.
"Apparently there is no smoking gun," said John Neuffer, political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute. "It's just bad PR (public relations)."

Many Japanese business executives also believe Hashimoto is convinced that reforms are vital. "If he's interested in the long-term, it is very apparent that he can't afford not to do it (reform) because the long-term future of Japan depends on this kind of deregulation and opening up markets," Hideo Ishihara, chairman of Goldman Sachs (Japan), told Reuters.
Still, many reform plans as yet fall short of the mark.
"The gun is being pointed in the direction of the private sector," Koll said of the financial reform plan.

"One-third of financial transactions are conducted through the public system (like the postal savings system). The issue is, will private financial firms still have to compete against a de facto subsidised public system, and unfortunately, the answer is 'yes,'" he said.

Signs have also emerged that the LDP may tone down proposals to strip the Finance Ministry of some of its power by creating an independent watchdog agency to oversee financial institutions -- perhaps partly because bureaucrats' backing is still crucial to crafting other reform plans.
The ministry came under fire for its handling of Japan's financial system woes and scandals involving senior officials.

"I think he (Hashimoto) too is playing a game because the bureaucrats have all the information and therefore in order to do real restructuring, he needs the cooperation of the bureaucrats," one Japanese businessman said.
